analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent FDA center to monitor drug safety after approval, with power to fine drugmakers and pull risky drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Democrat with one Republican cosponsor, was sent to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee in December 2005 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a drug is approved, the FDA would have had a permanent center whose job is to watch for new dangers, order follow-up studies, and act on what it finds. The center could force companies to run safety studies, fine them up to $2 million per 30-day period for refusing, require stronger warnings on ads for risky or newly approved drugs, and use expedited procedures to suspend or pull a drug off the market. It would also publish safety findings and study progress to the public every 90 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who takes prescription drugs, because dangerous side effects that only show up after millions of people use a drug would be detected and acted on faster, and the findings would be published openly.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Center for Postmarket Drug Evaluation and Research inside the FDA whose director must run ongoing risk assessment and surveillance of every approved drug and licensed biologic, rather than treating safety review as finished at approval.

Lets the director require postmarket safety studies, including comparative studies against other drugs, and contract with holders of patient databases for epidemiologic research, with a 90-day progress reporting requirement.

Allows corrective actions when a drug may pose an unreasonable risk — label changes, restricting which patients can use it, distribution limits, patient registries, and risk management plans — backed by civil penalties starting at $250,000 and doubling every 30 days of noncompliance, capped at $2 million per period.
Requires the FDA to publish, at least every 90 days, which studies were ordered, whether they are on schedule, and the agency's safety determinations with the supporting data and reasons.
Gives the director authority to withdraw or suspend a drug's approval through expedited procedures if its risk cannot be fixed by a corrective action or if the sponsor defies orders.

Makes the drug safety office an independent center reporting directly to the FDA Commissioner, rather than an office inside the drug approval center, so safety officials are not subordinate to the officials who approved the drug.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies, who would face mandatory safety studies, civil fines for noncompliance, required disclosures in advertising, and possible suspension or withdrawal of approvals. Taxpayers would fund the center through authorized appropriations starting at $50 million a year and rising to $150 million by 2010.

drawbacks.text: The program would be funded by taxpayers, with authorized appropriations rising from $50 million in fiscal 2006 to $150 million by fiscal 2010.

Drug sponsors would bear real compliance costs: required postmarket studies on deadlines set by the director, fines if studies slip, pre-clearance of all promotional material for flagged or newly approved drugs, and mandated public disclosures that could slow marketing of new products.

A fair concern: mandatory postmarket requirements and advertising restrictions raise the cost of bringing drugs to market, and a fair reading of the bill is that some of that cost could be passed along in drug prices; the bill does try to limit this by stating that preapproval review must not delay approval decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and ordinary: faster detection of drug dangers, real penalties for companies that stall, and public access to safety findings. The costs are real but conventional — a regulatory budget of up to $150 million a year and compliance costs for drugmakers — and the bill includes a safeguard against delaying approvals. On balance this is a straightforward consumer-safety bill whose costs fall mostly on the regulated industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2005, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Health Subcommittee in early December, and then sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the Food and Drug Administration Safety Act of 2005 on November 18, 2005, joined by Rep. Jim Ramstad.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced, and on December 2, 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
That was the last action ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, was never reported out of committee, and never came up for a vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

The bill attracted only three cosponsors — one Republican and two Democrats — beyond the sponsor, and it carried subjects including drug approvals, drug safety surveillance, civil penalties, and drug industry advertising.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies were better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory postmarket safety studies, civil penalties of up to $2 million per 30-day period, required disclosures in their advertising, and expedited withdrawal of approvals for drugs the agency judged unreasonably risky. Patients got no independent postmarket drug safety center from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmaceutical companies, by avoiding the oversight

for.name: Rep. John F. Tierney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create an independent FDA postmarket drug safety center with study, penalty, and withdrawal powers.

for.name: Rep. Jim Ramstad
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill on the day of introduction.

for.name: House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors to the bill.

against.name: Rep. Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it to a markup or a committee vote, and it died at the subcommittee stage.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on November 18, 2005 and referred it to the Subcommittee on Health on December 2, 2005; no further action was ever recorded on it.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill and recruited one Republican original cosponsor, with two more Democratic cosponsors; the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it, so the fight never produced a floor vote to measure.

industries.note: The bill would have required postmarket safety studies on deadlines set by regulators, imposed civil fines up to $2 million per 30-day period for noncompliance, allowed distribution restrictions and label changes for risky drugs, and permitted expedited suspension or withdrawal of approvals. Its death left companies without these new costs or enforcement tools.

For drugs with flagged safety issues or newly approved drugs, sponsors would have had to submit all promotional materials to the FDA 30 days before use and include prominent risk disclosures. That pre-clearance regime never took effect.

industries.industry: Holders of patient and surveillance databases
industries.note: The bill directs the FDA to contract with, or require drug sponsors to contract with, holders of domestic and international surveillance databases to run epidemiologic safety studies — a new revenue stream that died with the bill.
